name: pasta al funghi
instructions:
Traditional italian mushroom pasta — the leaner, more classically italian expression of 'creamy mushroom pasta' before it goes rich (see [[boscaiola]] for the cream + tomato + brandy woodsman-style rich variant). No cream, no tomato. Just mushrooms (fresh + dried porcini), garlic, wine, olive oil, parsley, and parmesan — the porcini + their soaking liquid are what carry it.

Untested by me. Written down as a scaffold worth trying. A slightly more built-out version than Marcella Hazan's minimalist take (fresh mushrooms + wine deglaze added on top of her dried-porcini base); see MARCELLA HAZAN REFERENCE note for context on why dried porcini is a foundational base in her repertoire.

SERVES 4.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 1 lb pasta — tagliatelle, fettuccine, or pappardelle (flat egg noodles are traditional here; the sauce is thin enough to want a ribbon shape)
- 1 oz (~30g) dried porcini mushrooms
- 1½ cups warm water OR warm chicken stock (for reconstituting the porcini — see PORCINI SECRET note)
- 1 lb fresh mushrooms (cremini + shiitake mix, or wild if you have them), sliced ¼-inch
- 3-4 tbsp olive oil (or half olive oil + half butter — see notes)
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- ½ cup dry white wine
- ¼ cup fresh italian parsley, minced
- ½ tsp fresh thyme (optional)
- ½ cup freshly grated parmigiano reggiano or pecorino romano
- salt and pepper
- reserved pasta water

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. RECONSTITUTE THE PORCINI: soak dried porcini in 1½ cups warm water (or warm chicken stock) for ~20 min until soft. Lift porcini out. STRAIN THE SOAKING LIQUID through a coffee filter or double layer of cheesecloth to remove grit — this liquid is your mushroom stock and it's what carries the dish. Roughly chop the reconstituted porcini.

2. BOIL SALTED PASTA WATER (2 tbsp kosher salt per gallon).

3. SEAR THE FRESH MUSHROOMS IN BATCHES: heat 2-3 tbsp olive oil in a large pan over medium-high. Add fresh mushrooms in a single layer (don't crowd — they'll steam not brown). Sear undisturbed until golden on one side, flip, brown the other side. Season with salt and pepper. Work in batches; transfer each batch to a plate.

4. GARLIC + PORCINI: reduce heat to medium. Add remaining olive oil (or butter). Sauté garlic 30 seconds — don't brown. Add the chopped reconstituted porcini and cook 1-2 min.

5. DEGLAZE WITH WINE: pour in the ½ cup dry white wine. Cook 1-2 min until reduced by half.

6. ADD THE PORCINI SOAKING LIQUID: pour in the strained porcini soaking liquid. Bring to a simmer. Cook 3-5 min until the liquid reduces to a light sauce consistency.

7. RETURN THE FRESH MUSHROOMS to the pan. Stir to coat in the sauce.

8. START PASTA: cook to 1 min less than al dente. Reserve ~1 cup pasta water before draining.

9. TOSS + FINISH: transfer drained pasta to the sauce pan. Toss to combine, adding splashes of reserved pasta water as needed to loosen. Off heat, stir in the parmigiano, minced parsley, and optional thyme. Serve immediately.
notes:
Traditional italian pasta al funghi. Untested by me — written down as a scaffold. The 'creamy mushroom pasta' family has this recipe as its lean/traditional pole and [[boscaiola]] as the rich/woodsman-style pole.

=== THE POINT — DRIED PORCINI + SOAKING LIQUID (THE 'SECRET') ===

The whole recipe depends on the combination of DRIED PORCINI + THEIR STRAINED SOAKING LIQUID:
- Dried porcini reconstitute into concentrated-flavor mushroom bits that fresh mushrooms can't match. They provide deep, dark umami — the fermented/dried process concentrates guanylates and glutamates that fresh porcini (rare to find fresh) or fresh cremini/shiitake can't produce.
- Their soaking liquid is a strong dark mushroom broth. Using it as the sauce stock is the whole secret — it's what makes the dish read deeply mushroomy without needing cream or tomato to carry it.

Skip the dried porcini or discard the soaking liquid and this recipe is just 'sautéed mushrooms with pasta' — fine but forgettable.

STRAIN THE SOAKING LIQUID through a coffee filter or double cheesecloth — dried porcini carry grit from the drying process that will settle in the bowl if unfiltered.

=== MARCELLA HAZAN REFERENCE — REEVALUATING THE POINT OF DRIED-ON-FRESH ===

Marcella Hazan's 'Fettuccine con i Funghi Porcini Secchi' (Fettuccine with Dried Porcini) from Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking is the canonical minimalist italian take: dried porcini + garlic + olive oil + parsley + tomato paste (sometimes) + pasta + parmesan. Very italian minimalism.

I've had that version and it tasted good — I just didn't initially see the point of combining mushrooms (or reconstituted-mushroom-bits) with what amounts to more mushroom flavor. It seemed redundant to double up. Revisiting Marcella now, I'm recognizing DRIED PORCINI (whole or as soaking liquid) as a foundational base ingredient across a lot of her recipes — the dried-porcini + fresh-mushroom (or dried-porcini + broth base) pattern shows up repeatedly and is doing structural flavor work, not just piling on. Worth understanding as a load-bearing italian technique rather than a novelty add.

WHY THIS VERSION IS SLIGHTLY MORE BUILT-OUT than Marcella's fettuccine con i funghi:
- FRESH MUSHROOMS IN ADDITION TO DRIED PORCINI — provides meaty chewy texture alongside the concentrated umami of the dried. Marcella's version uses only dried porcini; fresh + dried together gives you both dimensions.
- WHITE WINE DEGLAZE — adds acidity + depth.
- THYME OPTIONAL — a woodsy note that complements the mushroom register. Marcella uses only parsley.

The risk of over-building: pushing the dish into boscaiola territory (which is the cream + tomato + onion + brandy version). This recipe stops short of that — no cream, no tomato paste, no onion. Slightly richer than Marcella's minimalist frame, but still in traditional-italian-pasta-al-funghi territory rather than crossing into boscaiola.

Both are valid — Marcella's is the more traditional/austere version; this one adds body without breaking the frame.

=== NO CREAM, NO TOMATO — THAT'S BOSCAIOLA ===

Don't add cream. Don't add tomato paste. Both push the dish into [[boscaiola]] territory, which is a different (valid, but different) recipe.

The test of this recipe is whether the porcini + soaking liquid + fresh mushrooms can carry the sauce on their own. If they can, this is a proper pasta al funghi. If they can't, boscaiola is the fallback.

=== FRESH MUSHROOM CHOICE — CREMINI + SHIITAKE MIX OR WILD ===

Cremini + shiitake mix is the reliable default. Cremini provides bulk and familiar mushroom flavor; shiitake adds a more distinctive earthy-umami dimension.

IF WILD MUSHROOMS ARE AVAILABLE (chanterelle, black trumpet, morel, hen of the woods, oyster) — use them. This recipe's minimalist frame lets wild mushroom character shine in a way boscaiola's busier sauce doesn't.

LIONS MANE would also work here (the celebratory pick from the alfredo era).

=== HERBS — PARSLEY REQUIRED, THYME OPTIONAL ===

Parsley is the traditional finishing herb for pasta al funghi. Fresh italian parsley, minced, ¼ cup, added off heat.

Thyme (½ tsp fresh) is an optional woodsy add. Traditional italian pasta al funghi usually skips it; adding is fine.

NO ROSEMARY, NO BAY LEAF, NO SAGE — those are different italian traditions (rosemary is more mediterranean/roast, bay is stew, sage is butter/browned-butter pasta). None fit here.

=== OLIVE OIL vs BUTTER ===

Olive oil is the more traditional italian choice; butter (or half olive oil + half butter) reads slightly richer. Both work. Olive oil for the minimalist frame; butter or blended if you want more body.

=== FRESHLY GRATED PARMIGIANO OR PECORINO — NOT PRE-SHREDDED ===

Same rule as [[boscaiola]] — freshly grated. Pecorino romano is slightly sharper/saltier than parmigiano reggiano; either works.

=== HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM [[boscaiola]] ===

| Slot | This (pasta al funghi) | [[boscaiola]] |
|---|---|---|
| Cream | none | 1¼ cups heavy cream |
| Tomato paste | none | 3 oz |
| Onion | none | 1 medium diced |
| Alcohol | ½ cup white wine | 1 cup brandy |
| Mushroom liquid | strained porcini soaking liquid (concentrated) | pasta water only |
| Dried mushrooms | required (porcini) | not called for |
| Herb | parsley (+ optional thyme) | parsley |
| Character | lean, mushroom-forward, italian-minimalist | rich, layered, blush-boscaiola |

Different dishes; both valid corners of 'italian mushroom pasta.'

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- [[boscaiola]]: the rich woodsman-style pole. Cream + tomato paste + onion + brandy + mushrooms + parmesan.
- tomato pasta sauce family — [[marcella-tomato-sauce]], [[sicilian-pesto-rosso]], [[vodka-sauce]], [[pasta-piperade]], [[marcella-eggplant-sauce]] (all tagged 'tomato pasta sauce'): the strictly-tomato italian pasta sauce family. No cream/mushroom overlap but same pasta-with-real-sauce philosophy.
original_chef: Traditional italian pasta al funghi form. Built on Marcella Hazan's Fettuccine con i Funghi Porcini Secchi base (Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking) — dried porcini + garlic + olive oil + parsley + parmesan — with fresh mushrooms + white wine + optional thyme added on top for more sauce body. Dried porcini is a foundational base ingredient across Marcella's repertoire; the dried + fresh mushroom combination is a load-bearing italian technique, not a novelty add.
